content: Fluticasone nasal spray is prescribed to treat symptoms of seasonal allergic rhinitis (which occurs at specific times of the year), perennial allergic rhinitis (which occurs year-round), and perennial nonallergic rhinitis. These symptoms include sneezing, nasal congestion, runny nose, and nasal itching. Fluticasone belongs to a class of medications called corticosteroids. It works by reducing and preventing inflammation in the nasal passages, which helps alleviate these symptoms. Fluticasone nasal spray is available as a liquid that is sprayed into the nose. It is typically used once or twice daily, either in the morning and evening or as directed by your doctor. In some cases, it may be used only as needed to manage symptoms. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Use the medication exactly as prescribed. Do not use more or less of it or use it more frequently than directed by your doctor. This medication is intended for nasal use only. Do not swallow the spray or allow it to come into contact with your eyes. Your doctor may start you on a higher dose of fluticasone nasal spray and then reduce the dose once your symptoms are under control. While fluticasone helps manage the symptoms of rhinitis, it does not cure the condition. You may not notice improvement in your symptoms for at least 12 hours after the first use, and it may take several days or longer to experience the full benefits. For optimal results, use fluticasone regularly as part of a consistent schedule unless your doctor advises otherwise. Continue using the medication even if you feel well, and do not stop using it without consulting your doctor. Each bottle of fluticasone nasal spray is designed to deliver 120 sprays. After 120 sprays, the bottle may still contain some liquid, but the amount of medication in each spray may not be accurate. Keep track of the number of sprays you use and discard the bottle after 120 sprays, even if it still contains liquid. To use the nasal spray, follow these steps: 1. Shake the bottle gently. 2. Remove the dust cover. 3. If using the pump for the first time or after a week or more of non-use, prime it by pressing down and releasing the pump six times (or until a fine spray appears). 4. Blow your nose to clear your nostrils. 5. Close one nostril with your finger. 6. Tilt your head slightly forward and carefully insert the applicator into the other nostril, keeping the bottle upright. 7. Hold the pump with the applicator between your forefinger and middle finger and the bottom resting on your thumb. 8. Begin to breathe in through your nose. 9. While inhaling, press firmly down on the applicator to release a spray. 10. Breathe gently in through the nostril and exhale through your mouth. 11. If instructed to use two sprays in the same nostril, repeat steps 6–10. 12. Repeat the process for the other nostril. 13. Wipe the applicator with a clean tissue and replace the dust cover. This medication may also be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before using fluticasone nasal spray, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to fluticasone or any other medications. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking or have recently taken. Certain medications, such as antifungals, HIV protease inhibitors, and oral steroids, may interact with fluticasone, requiring dose adjustments or careful monitoring for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have or have ever had tuberculosis, cataracts, glaucoma, nasal sores, untreated infections, or herpes infections in the eye. Also, let your doctor know if you have recently had nasal surgery or an injury to your nose. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while using fluticasone, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform the doctor or dentist that you are using fluticasone. If you have been taking oral steroids, your doctor may gradually reduce your steroid dose after starting fluticasone. During this transition, your body may take several months to adjust, and conditions such as arthritis or eczema may worsen. Notify your doctor if this occurs or if you experience symptoms such as extreme fatigue, muscle weakness, sudden pain in the stomach or lower body, loss of appetite, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, fainting, depression, irritability, or darkened skin. Your body may also be less able to handle stress, such as surgery, illness, or severe asthma attacks, during this time. Inform all healthcare providers treating you that you recently switched from oral steroids to fluticasone. Carry a medical identification card or bracelet to alert emergency personnel that you may require steroid treatment in an emergency. Fluticasone may reduce your ability to fight infections. Avoid contact with sick individuals and wash your hands frequently. Stay away from people with chickenpox or measles, and inform your doctor immediately if you are exposed to these viruses. Discuss with your doctor whether you should avoid drinking grapefruit juice while using this medication. If you miss a dose, use it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not use a double dose to make up for a missed one. Fluticasone may cause side effects. Common minor side effects include headache, nosebleeds, nasal irritation, runny nose, bloody mucus, cough, upset stomach, vomiting, stomach pain, diarrhea, and dizziness. If these symptoms persist or worsen, inform your doctor. Serious side effects are rare but require immediate medical attention. These include painful white patches in the nose or throat, flu-like symptoms, sore throat, vision problems, nasal injuries, new or worsening acne, easy bruising, facial or neck swelling, extreme fatigue, muscle weakness, irregular menstrual periods, hives, rash, itching, swelling of the face or extremities, hoarseness, difficulty breathing or swallowing, and wheezing. Fluticasone may also slow growth in children. Discuss the risks with your child’s doctor. Store fluticasone in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for disposal instructions. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the individual collapses or is not breathing. Long-term overuse of fluticasone may cause symptoms such as facial or neck swelling, new or worsening acne, easy bruising, extreme fatigue, muscle weakness, irregular menstrual periods, loss of appetite, weight loss, irritability, depression, fainting, dizziness, or darkened skin. Keep all appointments with your doctor. Clean the nasal spray applicator weekly by removing the dust cap and applicator, washing them in warm water, letting them dry, and reassembling them. If the applicator becomes clogged, soak it in warm water, rinse it in cold water, and let it dry. Do not use sharp objects to clear blockages. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist with any questions about refills.
